 An extra hour offers a different perspective 
 JEWISH FEDERATION AT THE SHORE 
 By ohtadmin 
 on 
 November 11, 2026 
 RACHEL WALDMAN 
 Executive Director Jewish Federation of Atlantic & Cape May Counties 
 Twice a year, we collectively participate in a strange little ritual. We change our clocks, adjust our schedules, and spend the next several days trying to convince our bodies that the time is what the clock says it is.
 Daylight saving time came to an end at 2 a.m. on Sunday, Nov. 1. We turned our clocks back an hour, gaining 60 precious minutes of sleep (at least in theory). For parents of young children, of course, the promise of an extra hour of sleep is often more wishful thinking than reality.
 There is something peculiar about our relationship with time. We spend so much of our lives wishing we had more of it–more time with family, more time to accomplish our goals, more time to enjoy the things that make us happy. And yet, when we are handed an extra hour, we rarely know quite what to do with it.
 The tradeoff comes quickly. By late afternoon, darkness begins to settle over the shore. The long, sunlit evenings of summer feel like a distant memory, and suddenly we’re driving home from work beneath a dark sky. It’s a seasonal adjustment that can feel particularly dramatic here, where so much of our identity is tied to sunshine, beaches, and outdoor living.
 Jewish tradition has a particularly beautiful relationship with time. Our calendar is filled with opportunities to mark its passage, from the weekly rhythm of Shabbat to the changing seasons of our holidays. We don’t simply measure time by how much has passed. We give it meaning through what we choose to do with it.
 Perhaps that is the real opportunity this season offers.
 As the days grow shorter and the evenings become quieter, we have a chance to consider how we spend the hours we have. Maybe it’s an extra dinner together, a phone call to someone we haven’t spoken to in a while, attending a community program, or simply finding a few moments of peace in an otherwise busy day.
 We cannot actually create more time, no matter how many times we move the hands of a clock. But we can make the time we have count.
 And as we settle into November, with Thanksgiving approaching and Chanukah not far behind, I hope we can embrace the slower evenings, the opportunities for connection, and the warmth of community that makes this fall season special.
 After all, the best use of an extra hour might simply be spending it with someone who matters.
